strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: robustifying distilled students against covariate shift/spurious correlations when the shift is unknown and target groups are entirely absent from training data.

The proposed ConfiG method is intuitive and technically clear: it uses diffusion-guided latent optimization to maximize teacher confidence while minimizing student confidence, directly targeting the disagreement region between teacher and student decision boundaries.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet), multiple student architectures (ViT-T, TinyViT, ResNet-18), and various augmentation combinations (CutMix, MixUp, AutoAugment, CutMixPick), consistently showing gains especially in worst-group accuracy.

Thoughtful ablations: number of augmentations vs quality (showing that even 5-10x baseline augmentations cannot match 2x ConfiG augmentations), combination with model-centric bias mitigation (TAB), and computational cost analysis.
A theoretical proposition (with proof) offers formal justification for why confidence-guided augmentations reduce the covariate-shift-induced generalization gap under stated assumptions.

Qualitative visualizations (Fig. 3, 4, 6-8) clearly illustrate that ConfiG changes only spurious attributes while preserving causal class-relevant features, in contrast to baselines that either fail to alter spurious features or accidentally change the causal attribute.

Honest and clearly stated limitations regarding the necessity of a robust teacher, including an example where the CLIP teacher itself was insufficiently robust and a special fine-tuned teacher (using privileged balanced data) had to be substituted.
weaknesses: The experimental setting is fairly constructed/synthetic: training sets are small subsampled subsets (250-750 images/class) with deliberately and completely removed groups, which may not reflect realistic covariate shift severity or scale; it is unclear how results would transfer to larger, more naturally imbalanced datasets.

The method's core assumption -- availability of a teacher that is simultaneously robust to the (unknown) spurious features and well-calibrated -- is strong and, as acknowledged, not straightforward to satisfy in practice (e.g., CLIP's poor zero-shot performance on SpuCo Birds required an artificial workaround using a teacher fine-tuned with privileged balanced data, undermining the 'unknown shift, no group labels' framing for that dataset).

Computational overhead of ConfiG (11.4 s/image, ~3-5x costlier than baselines) is non-trivial, and while an ablation shows quality beats quantity, the added complexity of first training an auxiliary 'biased' student purely to generate augmentations adds an extra training stage that complicates the pipeline compared to single-shot augmentation baselines.

The methodological novelty is incremental relative to prior guided-diffusion counterfactual/disagreement generation work (e.g., DiG-IN, ActGen); the core contribution is largely combining an existing guided-diffusion framework with a teacher-confidence term and a nonlinear reweighting, which is a reasonable but modest algorithmic advance.

On Spurious ImageNet, gains are more marginal (ConfiG is only second-best in validation accuracy behind DAFusion, and mAUC improvements are within ~0.5-1%), suggesting the method's benefits may be most pronounced in the more contrived group-shift benchmarks rather than more realistic large-scale settings.

The theoretical analysis relies on several idealized assumptions (bounded teacher/student approximation errors, calibration, small deltas relative to 1/L) that are difficult to verify empirically, and the paper does not empirically validate how close real δs, δt are to satisfying the theorem's conditions, limiting the practical predictive value of the theory.

Some reported baseline variances are quite large (e.g., CutMixPick worst-group ±13.1), and no statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-tests) is reported to substantiate that ConfiG's improvements are significant beyond std overlap in a few cases.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: improving knowledge distillation robustness under covariate shift when spurious features are unknown and no group labels are available, distinguishing itself from prior group-robustness work that requires knowledge of relevant groups.

The proposed ConfiG method is conceptually clean: it leverages teacher-student disagreement to guide diffusion-based augmentation generation, directly targeting the student's reliance on spurious correlations rather than relying on student-only or data-only signals as in prior diffusion augmentation baselines (ActGen, DAFusion, DistDiff, GIF).

Strong and consistent empirical improvements across three datasets (CelebA, SpuCo Birds, Spurious ImageNet) and multiple architectures (ViT-T, TinyViT-11M, ResNet-18), with particularly large gains in worst-group accuracy (e.g., +12 points over the best baseline on CelebA worst-group accuracy).

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies: number of augmentations, cost-vs-quality trade-off showing ConfiG with fewer samples beats baselines with 5-10x more augmentations, compatibility with orthogonal model-centric debiasing methods (TAB), robustness to different student architectures, and larger training set sizes.

A theoretical proposition (Appendix A.1) formalizes the intuition for why confidence-guided augmentations reduce the covariate-shift-induced generalization gap, adding rigor beyond a purely empirical contribution.

Qualitative examples (Fig. 3, 4) are compelling and clearly illustrate how ConfiG alters spurious attributes while baselines fail to do so, including an interesting incidental finding of an unintentionally introduced spurious correlation (blond hair/blue eyes) that ConfiG also removes.
Transparent limitations discussion, including admission that the SpuCo Birds teacher required unrealistic fine-tuning access, and that CelebA student performance is bottlenecked by teacher quality.
weaknesses: ConfiG has substantially higher computational cost per image (11.4 sec/image vs. 2-3 sec for baselines) due to iterative decoding during optimization; while the cost-vs-quality ablation partially mitigates this concern, it still limits practical scalability to larger datasets/classes.

The theoretical guarantee (Proposition 1) relies on fairly strong and somewhat idealized assumptions (uniform bounds on teacher/student approximation error, small delta_s+delta_t<1/L, an implicit assumption that ConfiG-style augmentations lie exactly in the specified support region), making it more illustrative than a tight, verifiable guarantee in practice.

The method fundamentally depends on access to a teacher that is itself robust to the (unknown) covariate shift; the paper's own admission that a strong-enough CLIP teacher was unavailable for SpuCo Birds (requiring an unrealistic fine-tuned ViT-B teacher with access to a balanced dataset) raises questions about real-world applicability when such robust teachers are not readily available.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small/synthetic covariate-shift setups (500-1500 training images, subsampled 100-class ImageNet subset) rather than large-scale or naturally occurring shift scenarios, which somewhat limits the demonstrated generality of the approach.

Some results show high variance across seeds (e.g., CutMixPick worst-group std of 13.1 on CelebA), and only 3 training runs are used, which could weaken the statistical confidence of comparisons, particularly for close baseline comparisons like ActGen.

No systematic study of failure modes, e.g., what happens when the teacher is only partially robust, or quantitative image-quality/fidelity assessment of the generated augmentations beyond a handful of qualitative examples.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift, where certain test groups are entirely absent from training data, is a realistic and under-explored setting distinct from prior group-robustness work that assumes all groups are represented.

The proposed ConfiG method is technically well-designed, combining inter-class latent mixing (warm start) with confidence-guided latent optimization that explicitly maximizes teacher confidence while minimizing student confidence, directly targeting the teacher-student disagreement region motivated by the empirical analysis in Fig. 2/Table 1.

A theoretical analysis (Proposition 1 and supporting lemma) provides principled motivation for why augmentations that are more challenging for the student than the teacher can provably reduce the covariate-shift generalization gap, and the assumptions are discussed candidly, including their practical limitations.

Extensive, well-controlled experiments across four datasets (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, ImageNet-100) with six strong diffusion-based augmentation baselines, using FLOP-matched comparisons for fairness, and reporting mean/std over six training runs.

Very thorough ablation studies (individual components, replacement probability, number of augmentations, weaker teachers, alternative student/teacher architectures, single-step diffusion backbones, combination with model-centric bias-mitigation methods LfF/uLA, larger training sets, settings without covariate shift, target-class selection) that substantially strengthen the empirical case and probe robustness of the method.

Good qualitative analysis including failure case categorization and illustrative examples showing the mechanism (reduced student confidence while preserving teacher confidence, sometimes uncovering unintended spurious correlations).
weaknesses: Gains are inconsistent in magnitude across datasets/metrics: on BAR the SMA improvements over the strongest baseline are often small and within standard deviation, and Table 5 shows that combining real data with strong standard augmentations (MixUp/AutoAugment) can surpass ConfiG with only random-resized-crop augmentation on BAR, slightly undercutting the generality of the claimed benefit.

The pipeline is computationally and procedurally complex (null-text inversion + prompt-to-prompt inter-class mixing + iterative latent optimization with an auxiliary biased student), and although FLOP-matched comparisons are provided, the backward-pass FLOPs are only estimated (2x forward), and wall-clock/implementation complexity relative to baselines is not directly reported, which may affect reproducibility and practical adoption.

The theoretical result (Proposition 1) relies on several strong, hard-to-verify assumptions (bounded KL divergence of teacher from ground truth, well-calibrated teacher, controlled augmentation ratio alpha and confidence gap Theta); the authors themselves acknowledge that instantiating these constants or verifying the assumptions in practice is infeasible, which limits the practical predictive power of the theory beyond qualitative motivation.

Experiments are restricted to image classification with relatively small student backbones (ViT-Tiny, ConvNeXt-Atto); scalability to larger models/backbones or to other tasks (e.g., detection/segmentation) is not empirically demonstrated, and is explicitly deferred to future work.

The auxiliary-student-in-the-loop design (needed both for ConfiG and the ActGen baseline) introduces an additional training stage and dependency on how well this auxiliary model captures the spurious features, which is not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to auxiliary student quality/architecture) beyond the main results.

Given the face-attribute (CelebA-HQ) application generating synthetic demographic variations (gender, age, hair color), there is little explicit discussion of potential fairness or dataset-consent implications of synthesizing demographic attribute variations, beyond the brief limitations section.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: knowledge distillation under unknown covariate shift where entire test groups are absent from training data, illustrated clearly with the CelebA-HQ gender-classification example.

Novel technical contribution (ConfiG) that combines diffusion-based inter-class mixing with latent optimization explicitly maximizing teacher confidence while minimizing student confidence, directly targeting the student's blind spots without requiring explicit group labels.

Provides a theoretical justification (Proposition 1 and supporting lemma) showing under stated assumptions that augmentations which are more challenging for the student than the teacher provably shrink the generalization-error gap, and the paper is careful to discuss the practical limitations of this bound.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse datasets (CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR, ImageNet-100) and six strong diffusion-based augmentation baselines, with FLOP-matched comparisons for fairness.

Very thorough ablation suite: individual components (inter-class mixing vs. latent optimization), number of augmentations per image, replacement probability, weaker teachers, alternate student/teacher architectures, single-step diffusion backbones, larger training sets, combination with model-centric bias-mitigation methods (LfF, uLA), and a non-covariate-shift control setting (Oxford Pets).
Good qualitative analysis, including an honest discussion of failure cases and where the method's advantage narrows (e.g., BAR, larger SpuCo training sets).
High reproducibility: exhaustive appendix detailing hyperparameters, prompts, teacher inference setup, and computational cost accounting.
weaknesses: Gains are inconsistent on BAR (ConfiG is sometimes second-best to Diff-Mix in SMA), and improvements on some metrics fall within one standard deviation of the strongest baseline, slightly tempering the 'consistently best' framing in the main text.

The theoretical proposition relies on fairly strong/idealized assumptions (near-perfect calibrated teacher on both train and test, bounded KL divergence, controllable Θ and α), and the authors acknowledge these constants cannot be estimated or verified in practice, making the result primarily illustrative rather than actionable.

The method is computationally expensive relative to baselines (multi-step latent optimization plus an auxiliary student that must be trained per dataset), and although FLOPs are matched for fairness, wall-clock/training-pipeline overhead and practical scalability to datasets with many classes or larger images are not discussed.

Group-shift datasets are relatively small/curated (subsampled CelebA-HQ, SpuCo Birds, BAR) and require manual identification of descriptive vs. spurious attributes and prompt engineering (e.g., fine-grained species names for CLIP zero-shot on SpuCo Birds), which may limit generality to less curated real-world settings.

Reliance on an auxiliary student to guide generation assumes this student reliably captures the same spurious correlations as the final student; sensitivity of results to the auxiliary student's quality/architecture is not deeply analyzed.

Evaluation is restricted to image classification with small/light-weight backbones (ViT-T/S, ConvNeXt-Atto); applicability to larger-scale or non-classification tasks (noted as future work) remains unverified.
